title: Ethical Use of Technology in Digital Learning Environments: Graduate Student Perspectives
extended_summary:
This book-length open educational resource examines ethical issues related to technology use in digital learning environments, with chapters authored by graduate students in an ethics and technology course. The introduction describes a co-design process in which students, instructors, and other project collaborators jointly developed open Pressbooks chapters on topics including artificial intelligence, social networking, 3D printing, academic resource sharing, adaptive learning systems, STEM, assistive technologies, admissions, and fake news.

The AI-related chapter focuses specifically on ethical considerations when using artificial intelligence-based assistive technologies in education. It argues that AI tools can support personalized learning, assessment, and classroom efficiency, but only when teachers use them judiciously and with attention to privacy, informed consent, data security, transparency, and bias. The discussion emphasizes that these tools do not replace human teachers and that professional judgment remains central.

The relevant population is graduate students in a University of Calgary digital age program, though the content of the chapters ranges across K-12, higher education, and broader professional contexts. The work is primarily conceptual and reflective rather than empirical, using Farrow’s ethics framework to guide analysis. Its main conclusion is that educational technologies, including AI-based assistive tools, should be implemented with strong ethical safeguards, clear policies, and awareness of how data collection and algorithmic systems may affect learners and teachers.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/reflective book chapter rather than an empirical study. It does not present a clear research design, comparison group, or measured outcomes, so it does not meet criteria for experimental or observational evidence tiers.
impact_tier_rationale: The chapter has likely educational relevance for guiding implementation and policy discussions around AI in classrooms, but it reports no direct measured impact. Any impact is indirect and theoretical rather than demonstrated through outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ethics-focused discussion of AI-based assistive technologies in education, including speech-to-text, predictive text, grading software, and personalized learning tools used by teachers and students
